title: The summit
hook: five years of mornings; the Buddha said he only shows the way, and you walked it
tomorrow: the summit's behind you. so where does the path go from here?

segments.voice: Last night, the night under the tree: he sat through three watches and didn't get up. Stay put. This morning, the top, and one question: whose steps carried you up.

A map app can show the whole route, every turn glowing blue. It has never walked anyone home. A brahmin accountant named Moggallana put that problem to the Buddha. You teach the path step by step, he said. Nibbana exists, the path exists, you're the guide. So does everyone you teach get there? Some do, the Buddha said. Some don't. Then why, asked the accountant, when everything's laid out? Five years of mornings end with his answer.
screen: `THE MAP NEVER WALKS.` → `AN ACCOUNTANT'S QUESTION.` → `SOME DO, SOME DON'T.` → `WHY?`

segments.voice: The Buddha answered with a question. You know the road to Rajagaha? Someone asks you the way, and you tell them exactly: follow this road, you'll see a village, then a town, then the city and its parks. One follows it and arrives. One takes the wrong road. What can you do? You're one who shows the way. So it is with me, the Buddha said: the Tathagata shows the way. The Dhammapada says it in Max Müller's words: "You yourself must make an effort. The Tathâgatas (Buddhas) are only preachers." That's the teaching at the top. The Buddha is a guide, not a ride; the walking belongs to the walker. A neighbor's book, from China, has its own step. In the Tao Te Ching, as James Legge translated it, Laozi writes that "the journey of a thousand li commenced with a single step." Both picture a long way crossed one step at a time. Where they part: for Laozi the Tao is the nameless way of heaven and earth, followed by not forcing; for the Buddha the path is a road a teacher points out, to the end of dukkha. Look back down the slope: the four truths, the immeasurables, the good given away, the path ahead, the night under the tree. He pointed. You walked it.
screen: `THE ROAD TO RAJAGAHA.` · `THE TATHAGATA SHOWS THE WAY.` · `A THOUSAND LI, ONE STEP.` · `HE POINTED; YOU WALKED.` · then, large: `YOU WALKED IT.`

segments.voice: Sit for most of the time, nothing to fix, nowhere to get to. In the last moments, turn toward a window or a door and look out, as far as you can see. That's the view from five years of mornings, and the road keeps going past it.
The summit: five years of mornings, and the view from the top. The Buddha showed the way. The steps were yours.
Take this one down the mountain: you walked it. He pointed; the walking was yours. Fourteen of fourteen, and the path goes on.

screen: `DAY 1791 COUNTS.` → `THE SUMMIT · 14 OF 14.` → `TOMORROW: THE SUMMIT'S BEHIND YOU. WHERE DOES THE PATH GO?`

howItsDone: Buddhists honor the Buddha as the one who showed the way, and Dhammapada 276 is one of the verses that says so: teachers and the sangha guide, but the practice is one's own.

match.prompt: the view from the top — tap the pairs.
pairs: directions given; walking is up to you
a thousand li begins with one step

myth: the Moggallana in this sutta is the Buddha's famous chief disciple
he's a brahmin accountant, Ganaka Moggallana; the chief disciple only shares the name.
the Dhammapada calls the Tathagatas only preachers
in Max Müller's translation: you yourself must make an effort.

fork.setup: a friend says, 'if the Buddha was a real teacher, everyone he taught would have reached nibbana.' what does the accountant's question say back?
options: a guide can give exact directions; arriving still takes the walker's steps.
everyone he taught did arrive; the sutta just doesn't list them.
he kept the last turn hidden, so only the best students would find it.
fork.reveal: the Buddha said plainly: some do, some don't. he shows the way, like directions to Rajagaha; the walking is each person's.

original.note: Pali, Dhammapada 276: the Tathagatas only tell the way.

trapdoor: what you thought: the summit is the finish, where you get to stop.
what it means: the top after five years of mornings, where you see the Buddha showed the way and you walked it.
what a scholar hears: Majjhima Nikaya 107's road to Rajagaha and Dhammapada 276, akkhataro tathagata: the Tathagatas only tell the way.
guess: the top after five years: he showed the way, you walked it
a mountain shrine where the Buddha's relics are kept
the final vow a monk takes before teaching others

chat.says: GRADUATED. slept fine, actually. ông says 'you walked it.' but he drove me to the chùa for years??
options: both: in the sutta the Buddha shows the way and each one walks it. ông showed; you walked.
then it's really ông's win; a student just follows, so the credit is his.
it's all yours; once you get there, the people who guided you stop mattering.
chat.meaning: The Buddha told the accountant he is one who shows the way; whoever follows the directions arrives. Guide and walker both count.

tie.story: The Buddha told Moggallana the accountant he only shows the way, like giving directions to Rajagaha.
tie.friend: Ông showed Mai the road for years; on graduation day he's telling her the steps were hers.
tie.you: who showed you the way, and which steps were yours?

Moggallana.meaning: here, a brahmin accountant, not the famous disciple

Rajagaha.meaning: a city where the Buddha often stayed

Tathagata.meaning: the thus-gone one: the Buddha's name for himself

Laozi.meaning: the Chinese sage tradition credits with the Tao Te Ching

li.meaning: an old Chinese measure of distance

Tao.meaning: Chinese for the way: in Laozi, the nameless way of things

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 107 (Ganakamoggallana Sutta: the road to Rajagaha; the Tathagata only shows the way)

notes: MN 107 paraphrased: the brahmin Ganaka Moggallana (the accountant, not the chief disciple) asks whether all disciples attain nibbana; some do, some don't; the road-to-Rajagaha simile (a village, then a town, then Rajagaha with its parks); 'the Tathagata is one who shows the way'. Confirm the details of the directions.
Dhammapada 276 quoted from Max Müller 1881 with his parenthesis; confirm exact wording. Original-language line akkhataro tathagata (अक्खातारो तथागता) from the Pali verse; confirm.

Unity thread (wisdom day): Tao Te Ching 64 quoted from Legge 1891 ('the journey of a thousand li commenced with a single step'); confirm exact wording. Shared: a long way walked step by step by the walker. Honest difference: Laozi's Tao as the nameless way of heaven and earth, followed by not forcing (ch. 1, paraphrased), vs. the Buddha's path pointed out by a teacher to the end of dukkha. No ranking. A Keeper may prefer a different neighbor; Taoism is chosen because Vietnamese Buddhist families often live alongside Taoist and Confucian teaching, which is kept out of the spoken text.

Last day of the block and the year: the teach looks back over this week's words (four truths, immeasurables, dedication, ahead, the night). The 'tomorrow' line is a teaser past the final day; if no day 1792 exists, the app may show it as an open question.
Practice: sit, then look out (outline). 'Look at one object' used twice in seven days (1787, 1791).
Shape: wisdom (who walks the path?). Answers day 1790's tomorrow. Mai's storyline ends: she sleeps, graduates, and ông tells her she walked it.
Surprising fact: the Buddha told a questioner plainly that not everyone he taught reached the goal; he only shows the way.
